issuer: Georgia Government Transparency and Campaign Finance Commission
title: Georgia Advisory Opinion 2017-05
text:
GEORGIA GOVERNMENT TRANSPARENCY & CAMPAIGN FINANCE COMMISSION
ADVISORY OPINION NO. 2017-05
In response to five questions submitted to the Commission regarding the legality of candidates or their committees creating or contributing to nonprofit entities that may engage in advocacy directly or indirectly related to the candidate’s campaign, the Commission opines that other than creating a campaign committee as permitted by law, neither a candidate nor the candidate’s campaign committee may establish, operate, solicit donations for, nor coordinate communications with a nonprofit or other entity that expends money for communications referring to the candidate or the candidate’s opponent. In such instances of solicitation and coordination, the expenditures on the communications are contributions to the candidate reportable on the candidate’s or candidate committee’s Campaign Contribution Disclosure Report (“CCDR”). This result pertains regardless of whether the communications are “express advocacy,” regardless of whether the entity was initially created as an “independent committee,” and regardless of the specific federal tax section under which the entity is formed or with which it intends to comply. The answer to the specific questions is, of course, controlled by the specifics of the detailed overview and discussion of the issues, below.
Questions Presented
In a letter from Douglas Chalmers of Douglas, Pak, Burch & Adams, LLC, the following specific questions were presented for an advisory opinion from the Commission:
(1) May a candidate and/or his or her agents directly or indirectly establish, operate, and/or solicit funds for a nonprofit corporation or other entity that will make expenditures for public communications that will reference that candidate, and/or that candidate’s opponent(s) in an election, if those communications do not contain express advocacy?
(2) Does the answer to Question #1 turn in any way on whether the entity described has been established as a political organization under Section 527 of the Internal Revenue Code, meaning that it has been established for the primary purpose of influencing elections?
(3) If a candidate and/or his or her agents solicit contributions to the type of entity described in Question #1, are such contributions regulated or limited by the Act or the Rules?
(4) May a candidate and/or his or her agents coordinate (as that concept is applied in the Rules) with an entity of the type described in Question #1 on expenditures for public communications that will reference that candidate, or that candidate’s opponents(s) in an election, if those communications do not contain express advocacy? In other words, may a candidate and/or his or her agents request or suggest that such an entity make such expenditures, or cooperate or consult with the entity with respect to such expenditures? If such expenditures are coordinated in such a way with the candidate and/or his or her agents, are such expenditures regulated or limited by the Act or the Rules?
(5) May a candidate and/or his or her agents establish, create and/or solicit contributions for an independent committee that will make expenditures for communications that expressly advocate the election of that candidate if neither the candidate nor his or her agents coordinate with the independent committee on the expenditures themselves?
Background and Overview of the Law
The question of the extent a candidate may create or coordinate campaign activities or communications with other organizations that advocate related to his or her campaign is one rapidly rising in national prominence. At the federal level this issue is partly controlled by (and is enmeshed with) federal tax law, which currently permits different types of nonprofit organizations directly or indirectly related to campaigns or political issues and has disclosure rules regarding such nonprofits’ donors and limits on the nonprofits’ political activities. See, e.g., 26 U.S.C. §§ 501(c)(3) (religious, charitable, scientific, and educational groups, which may, among other things, engage in voter registration, and limited lobbying but otherwise no political activity), 501(c)(4) (non-profit social welfare groups not required to publicly disclose their donors and who may engage in some political activity relevant to their purpose or members if doing so is not their primary purpose), 501(c)(5) (labor and agricultural groups, which may perform some political activities related to their members’ common interests and are not required to publicly disclose their donors), 501(c)(6) (business leagues, chambers of commerce, real estate organizations and trade boards, which may perform some political activities related to their members’ common interests and are not required to publicly disclose their donors), 527 (“political organizations” that are organized and operate to influence elections and must disclose their donors).
Of note among these groups are so-called “Super PACs,” which are § 527 organizations that do not coordinate their activities with a candidate and, in light of this non-coordination, may receive unlimited contributions and make unlimited expenditures. The wide use of “Super PACs” arose from the United States Supreme Court’s decision in Citizens United v. FEC, 558 U.S. 310 (2009) (holding inter alia that the First Amendment permits unlimited corporate funding of independent political broadcasts in candidate elections although it is lawful to require that donors be disclosed) and SpeechNow.org v. FEC, 599 F.3d 686 (D.C. Cir. 2010) (holding unconstitutional contribution limits on a § 527 organization that engaged in “express advocacy” not coordinated with a candidate and otherwise upholding federal donor disclosure and other reporting requirements on the organization). Following these cases, it is now established that federal and state elections commissions may regulate some aspects of organizations that make independent expenditures and engage in express advocacy but they may not limit the size of contributions to or expenditures by such organizations.
Georgia law is similar to but does not mirror federal campaign finance law. Georgia law defines a “political action committee” (referred to herein and elsewhere as a “PAC”) as:
(A) Any committee, club, association, partnership, corporation, labor union, or other group of persons which receives donations during a calendar year from persons who are members or supporters of the committee and which contributes funds to one or more candidates for public office or campaign committees of candidates for public office; and
(B) A “separate segregated fund” as defined in Code Section 21-5-40. Such term does not include a candidate campaign committee.
O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(20).
Since PACs, by definition, are organizations that “contribute[] funds to one or more candidates,”
O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(20), they are governed by the contribution limits imposed by Georgia law.
O.C.G.A. § 21-5-41. In addition, if they make more than $25,000 in “aggregate contributions and expenditures to or on behalf of candidates,” they must register with the Commission and file CCDRs. O.C.G.A. § 21-5-34(e).
An “independent committee,” on the other hand, is:
any committee, club, association, partnership, corporation, labor union, or other group of persons, other than a campaign committee, political party, or political action committee, which receives donations during a calendar year from persons who are members or supporters of the committee and which expends such funds either for the purpose of affecting the outcome of an election for any elected office or to advocate the election or defeat of any particular candidate.
O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(15).
While Georgia law imposes registration and donor/expenditure disclosure requirements on independent committees, it does not impose caps on the amount of contributions or expenditures they may make. See O.C.G.A. § 21-5-34(f). That is because “independent committees” do not make contributions directly to candidates. See id. In this regard, the Commission’s regulations provide that
Campaign contribution limits on contributions to candidates do not apply to independent expenditures made to influence candidate elections. An independent expenditure is an expenditure for a communication which expressly advocates the election or defeat of a clearly identified candidate but which is made independently of any candidate’s campaign. However, an expenditure is “independent” only if it meets certain conditions. It must not be made with the cooperation or consent of, or in consultation with, or at the request or suggestion of any candidate or any of his or her agents or authorized committees. An expenditure which does not meet the above criteria for independence is considered a contribution which is subject to limits.
Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 189-3-.01(f).
Similarly, the Commission’s regulations define an “independent expenditure” as a political campaign communication that expressly advocates the election or defeat of a clearly identified candidate that is not made in cooperation, consultation, or concert with or at the request or suggestion of a candidate or candidate’s authorized committees.
Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 189-2-.01(12).
In two advisory opinions the Commission expressly limited independent committees to organizations that “expressly advocate,” referring to this as the “express advocacy standard set out in Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1, at 44 (1976) … .” AO 2001-32; see also AO 2010-05 (reaffirming A0 2001-32 and its reference to Buckley v. Valeo). Buckley v. Valeo’s specific formulation of “express advocacy” was 35 years old at the time AO 2001-32 was issued, and it was outdated and superseded as a constitutional standard at the time AO 2010-05 was issued. See McConnell v. FEC, 540 U.S. 93, 192-93 (2003); 11 C.F.R. 100.22 (current federal regulatory definition of “expressly advocating”).
This raises the question, however, of when communications and similar activity that are not express advocacy nonetheless constitute a “contribution” to a candidate. Under the Campaign Finance Act a “contribution” is defined, in pertinent part, as:
[A] gift, subscription, membership, loan, forgiveness of debt, advance or deposit of money or anything of value conveyed or transferred for the purpose of influencing the nomination for election or election of any person for office …. The term specifically shall not include the value of personal services performed by persons who serve without compensation from any source and on a voluntary basis. The term “contribution” shall include other forms of payment made to candidates for office or who hold office when such fees and compensation made can be reasonably construed as a campaign contribution designed to encourage or influence a candidate or public officer holding elective office. …
O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(7) (emphasis added); cf. O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(12) (similar language in definition of “expenditure”).
The Commission’s regulations state regarding “in-kind contributions” that:
(1) An in-kind contribution is deemed a “contribution” for purposes of the Act, and refers to any item of value other than money received by a candidate or any committee.
(2) The aggregate of monetary and in-kind contributions from the same contributor shall not exceed the maximum contribution limits authorized by the Act.
Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 189-6-.07.
Similarly, they define “In-kind expenditure” as:
An expenditure of any goods or services for which a candidate or campaign committee did not extend payment to an end-recipient for the goods or services provided, but for which the campaign received the use / benefit of said goods or services (e.g., A computer is loaned to the campaign and the computer is returned to the donor upon the conclusion of the campaign).
Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 189-2-.01(11).
A paradigmatic example of an “in-kind” expenditure is printing campaign signs for a candidate. See, e.g., In re: Michael Payne, case no. 2007-0023 before the Commission. Such signs are “speech,” and so it is evident that under some circumstances speech or communications by a third party can constitute in-kind contributions. Of course, typically campaign signs are both “express advocacy” by anyone’s standard and, moreover, are coordinated with a candidate. Yet, it is possible that there are instances where communications (whether particularly obscure signs or something else) might not be “express advocacy” under a narrow definition of the phrase and yet still be communications made “for the purpose of influencing the nomination for election or election of any person for office” — that is, within the scope of Georgia’s statutory definition of a “contribution.” O.C.G.A. § 21-5-3(7). In this instance, while the communication is not one of an “independent committee,” as there is no express advocacy, it may, nonetheless, be an in-kind contribution to a campaign. The evidence that it is an in-kind contribution to a campaign is strongest when the communication was made at the behest of or in coordination with the candidate. That is, if a candidate asks for a communication or speech of some sort, the cost of providing it may be an “in-kind” contribution to the candidate regardless of whether the speech was “express advocacy.” Cf. FEC v. Colo. Republican Fed. Campaign Comm., 533 U.S. 431, 442, 446 (2001) (the effect of coordination between candidates and outside supporters fundamentally transformed the expenditure, noting a “wink or nod” often will be “as useful to the candidate as cash.”).
Against this background, then, we consider the specific questions presented.
Discussion of the Specific Questions Presented
(1) May a candidate and/or his or her agents directly or indirectly establish, operate, and/or solicit funds for a nonprofit corporation or other entity that will make expenditures for public communications that will reference that candidate, and/or that candidate’s opponent(s) in an election, if those communications do not contain express advocacy?
In considering this question it must be noted at the outset that it overtly assumes that the communications made are not “express advocacy.” Therefore, under the Commission’s existing advisory opinions, the third person entity would not be an independent committee since an independent committee must, among other things, engage in express advocacy. AO 2001-32; AO 2010-05. Nonetheless, the question also assumes that the communications “reference that candidate, and/or that candidate’s opponent(s),” a situation that is often “express advocacy.” In other words, while the question disclaims express advocacy, it presents a fact situation that could well be express advocacy.
Georgia law currently provides a mechanism for candidates to create and operate an entity that advocates on their behalf: a campaign committee. O.C.G.A. § 21-5-30(a). The law permitting a candidate to have a campaign committee expressly provides that “no contributions to bring about the nomination or election of a candidate for any office shall be made or accepted except directly to or by a candidate or such candidate’s campaign committee which is organized for the purpose of bringing about the nomination or election of any such candidate … .” Id.
In providing candidates with the option of creating a campaign committee, the General Assembly has provided a singular mechanism by which “a candidate [may] … establish, operate, and/or solicit funds for [an] … entity that will make expenditures for public communications that will reference that candidate, and/or that candidate’s opponent(s) in an election …” per the question presented. This is patently one organization that operates on the candidate’s behalf: it is referred to in the singular and is required to have a unique bank account and to report and file with the Commission as part of the candidate’s filings. O.C.G.A. § 21-5-30. In referring to “campaign committee” in the singular throughout the Campaign Finance Act and in only providing for the creation of one campaign committee for a candidate, the Act perforce excludes the possibility that a candidate may create and operate multiple entities on his or her behalf. Cf. Mooney v. Webster, 300 Ga. 283, 288 (2016) (Supreme Court of Georgia follows “the long-recognized doctrine of statutory construction, expressio unius est exclusio alterius”). The Act does not provide for a candidate to have multiple campaign committees, nor does it allow or provide a mechanism for candidates to operate their campaigns and avoid lawful reporting to the Commission by creating entities that are not campaign committees. Indeed, as quoted above, the Act expressly prohibits “contributions to bring about the nomination or election of a candidate for any office” that are not made “directly to or by a candidate or such candidate’s campaign committee which is organized for the purpose of bringing about the nomination or election of any such candidate.” O.C.G.A. § 21-5-30(a).
For this same reason it would not be lawful for a candidate to solicit funds for a nonprofit or other entity “that will reference that candidate, and/or that candidate’s opponent(s) in an election,” even if the candidate has not created or in control of that organization, if funds solicited are “to bring about the nomination or election of a candidate for any office.” The Act requires such contributions to go to the candidate or the candidate’s committee, and a candidate cannot solicit the funds to go to a different organization than the candidate’s committee. Id.
Finally, it must be noted that the question presented refers to communications that “reference that candidate, and/or that candidate’s opponent(s) in an election … .” (Emphasis added.) There may be appropriate instances where “a candidate and/or his or her agents directly or indirectly establish, operate, and/or solicit funds for a nonprofit corporation,” per the question, that happens to refer to the candidate or the candidate’s opponent but which are not “to bring about the nomination or election of a candidate for any office,” per O.C.G.A. § 21-5-30(a). This opinion does not address such activity.
(2) Does the answer to Question #1 turn in any way on whether the entity described has been established as a political organization under Section 527 of the Internal Revenue Code, meaning that it has been established for the primary purpose of influencing elections?
The answer to Question #1, above, does not turn on whether the outside entity is a § 527 organization or not. Regardless of whether an organization has been created under federal tax law (or corresponding provisions in the federal elections code) for the primary purpose of influencing elections, if the actual conduct or communications in question are “to bring about the nomination or election of a candidate for any office” then the answer to Question #1, above, applies.
(3) If a candidate and/or his or her agents solicit contributions to the type of entity described in Question #1, are such contributions regulated or limited by the Act or the Rules?
The only lawful way a candidate may solicit contributions during a campaign to support the candidate’s election11 is by and for the candidate or the candidate’s campaign committee. O.C.G.A.
§ 21-5-30(a). The candidate or the candidate’s campaign committee are regulated by the Campaign Finance Act and Commission’s rules, and the amount of contributions they may receive (and in some instance the source of those contributions) are limited by law. See O.C.G.A. §§ 21-5-30.1, 21-5-41. The outcome if a candidate has violated the law is outside of the scope of this opinion and dependent on the specific facts presented in such an instance, and it may be subject to civil penalty pursuant to O.C.G.A. § 21-5-6(b)(14)(C) and or prosecution pursuant to O.C.G.A. § 21-5-9, among other possible remedies or actions.
(4) May a candidate and/or his or her agents coordinate (as that concept is applied in the Rules) with an entity of the type described in Question #1 on expenditures for public communications that will reference that candidate, or that candidate’s opponents(s) in an election, if those communications do not contain express advocacy? In other words, may a candidate and/or his or her agents request or suggest that such an entity make such expenditures, or cooperate or consult with the entity with respect to such expenditures? If such expenditures are coordinated in such a way with the candidate and/or his or her agents, are such expenditures regulated or limited by the Act or the Rules?
Under Georgia law, if a candidate coordinates with a nonprofit or other organization on campaign communications or activities, then the expenditures for the communications or activities are likely in-kind contributions to the candidate. See pp. 4-6, supra (discussing in-kind contributions). As contributions to a candidate, they are subject to the contribution limitations under Georgia law.
O.C.G.A. § 21-5-41.
Such a situation is, in fact, contemplated by the Commission’s regulations:
Campaign contribution limits on contributions to candidates do not apply to independent expenditures made to influence candidate elections. An independent expenditure is an expenditure for a communication which expressly advocates the election or defeat of a clearly identified candidate but which is made independently of any candidate’s campaign. However, an expenditure is “independent” only if it meets certain conditions. It must not be made with the cooperation or consent of, or in consultation with, or at the request or suggestion of any candidate or any of his or her agents or authorized committees. An expenditure which does not meet the above criteria for independence is considered a contribution which is subject to limits.
Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 189-3-.01(f) (emphasis added). See also Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 189- 2-.01(12) (an “independent expenditure” … “is not made in cooperation, consultation, or concert with or at the request or suggestion of a candidate or candidate’s authorized committees.”).
A purported “independent committee” or other political organization that consults with a candidate in making such expenditures has converted itself to a PAC, at least for the purpose of those expenditures. If it exceeds $25,000 in such contributions, it must register and file CCDRs as a contributor. O.C.G.A. § 21-5-34(e). Likewise, such expenditures are contributions to the candidate and must be duly reported on the candidate’s CCDR.
(5) May a candidate and/or his or her agents establish, create and/or solicit contributions for an independent committee that will make expenditures for communications that expressly advocate the election of that candidate if neither the candidate nor his or her agents coordinate with the independent committee on the expenditures themselves?
In responding to Question #5, above, it must be noted that, prior to taking steps to run for office (including collecting or expending funds to run for office), a potential candidate may engage in this activity, and it is a commonplace occurrence, particularly in the arena of federal elections. In such situations, once the candidate has taken steps that bring the candidate within the governing campaign finance law (and that varies between state and federal elections), then the coordination ceases and the entity created functions — at least in theory — independently of the candidate.
If a candidate attempts to establish or obtain funding for such a purported “independent committee” after the candidate beings campaigning — that is, the candidate falls within the ambit of the Campaign Finance Act by accepting contributions or making expenditures, O.C.G.A. §§ 21- 5-3(7), (12), 21-5-30(b) — then the establishment of the committee by the candidate is per se a form of coordination with the committee. In such an instance, the purported “independent committee” would be a contributor — i.e. a PAC and not an independent committee — as the expenditures by the entity cannot be “independent expenditures.” That is, they would per se “be made with the cooperation or consent of, or in consultation with, or at the request or suggestion of any candidate or any of his or her agents or authorized committees.” Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 189-3-.01(f); 189-2-.01(12). A candidate who seeks contributions to an “independent committee” for the purpose of its advocacy in the candidate’s campaign is consenting to those communications and, indeed, is suggesting that they be made.
As discussed above, such expenditures are contributions to the candidate and must be duly reported on the candidate’s CCDR. Likewise, the entity exceeds $25,000 in such contributions, it must register and file CCDRs as a contributor.
Conclusion
For the forgoing reasons, the Georgia Government Transparency & Campaign Finance Commission advises that, other than creating a campaign committee as permitted by law, neither a candidate nor the candidate’s campaign committee may establish, operate, solicit donations for, nor coordinate communications with a nonprofit or other entity that expends money for communications referring to the candidate or the candidate’s opponent. In instances of such solicitation and coordination, the expenditures on the communications are contributions to the candidate reportable on the candidate’s or candidate committee’s CCDR. This result pertains regardless of whether the communications are “express advocacy,” regardless of whether the entity was initially created as an “independent committee,” and regardless of the specific federal tax section under which the entity is formed or with which it intends to comply.
This Advisory Opinion concerns the application of the Georgia Government Transparency and Campaign Finance Act, or regulations prescribed by the Georgia Government Transparency and Campaign Finance Commission, to the specific facts, transaction or activity set forth supra.
Advisory Opinion 2017-05 is hereby adopted by the Commission in conformity with O.C.G.A. § 21-5-6(13) on _____________ , 2017.
Mary Paige Adams Chair of the Commission
